a: with the east wind
p: The hot, dry wind off the desert. Eliphaz says Job's words are like it: loud, scorching and empty.
b: The east wind (qadim) blows in off the Arabian desert, hot and dry, and withers plants in a day (Genesis 41:6; Ezekiel 17:10; Jonah 4:8). In Job it is a destroying wind (27:21; 38:24). Eliphaz turns the old charge back at Job: in 8:2 Bildad called Job's words "a mighty wind", and Job himself had said that the words of a desperate man are only wind (6:26). Now Eliphaz says a wise man would not fill his "belly", the seat of thought, with such wind. Job throws the phrase straight back in 16:3.

a: Worse, you are undoing reverence
p: Eliphaz accuses Job of more than his own sin: his talk tears down other people's fear of God and their prayer.
b: The Hebrew says simply "fear" (yir'ah), but in Job the word means reverence for God, as when Eliphaz first asked whether Job's fear of God was not his confidence (4:6). Siach, here "prayer", can mean musing, complaint or devotion; Job uses it for his own "complaint" (7:13; 10:1; 21:4). Eliphaz's point is that Job's speeches are dangerous to others. If a man known for his goodness says that God is unjust, he weakens the piety of everyone who hears him. A first reader would have felt the weight of this charge: a teacher who undermines faith harms the community.

a: you have picked the speech of the cunning
p: The word for 'cunning' is the word used for the snake in Eden.
b: 'Arumim, "the cunning", is the plural of 'arum, the word for the snake that was "shrewder than every wild animal of the field" (Genesis 3:1). Eliphaz used it before of the schemers whom God traps (5:12–13). In Proverbs it can be a good word, meaning shrewd or prudent (Proverbs 12:16; Proverbs 14:15), but here it is the smooth talker. The first line is also two-sided: "your guilt teaches your mouth" (the Plain, with most translators) or "your mouth teaches your guilt", that is, your words show what you have done (so the KJV, "thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity").

a: Was it you, born the first of humankind?
t: The first man and wisdom born before the hills
p: Eliphaz mocks Job as if he claimed to be the wise first human, born before the hills like Wisdom in Proverbs 8.
b: Two old pictures stand behind the taunt. One is the first human as a figure of perfect wisdom, as in Ezekiel's lament for the king of Tyre, "full of wisdom" in Eden on the mountain of God (Ezekiel 28:12–15). The other is Wisdom herself, who says she was "birthed" before the mountains and the hills, using the same verb, cholal (Proverbs 8:24–25). Eliphaz asks whether Job thinks he is that primal sage. Some scholars see a link with myths of a first man who stole wisdom from the gods, such as the Mesopotamian Adapa; the parallel is loose, and the verse needs only the biblical pictures to make sense.
orig: הֲרִאישׁוֹן אָדָם תִּוָּלֵד (hari'shon adam tivvaled), 'were you born the first human?'

a: Were you a listener at God's council?
p: Sod is the inner circle where God's plans are discussed, the heavenly council of 1:6.
b: Sod means a close circle of advisers and what is said there: both the council and its secrets. The prophets claim to have "stood in the council of the LORD" (Jeremiah 23:18, 22), and Amos says God does nothing without revealing his sod to the prophets (Amos 3:7). Job's readers have already seen that council meet, with the Accuser among the sons of God (1:6; 2:1), a scene Job never sees. Eliphaz's question is ironic: no human in the book has heard what was said there, Eliphaz included.
orig: סוֹד אֱלוֹהַּ (sod Eloah), 'the council of God'

a: Is the comfort God gives too little for you
p: Eliphaz probably means his own first speech, which he offered as comfort from God.
b: The friends came "to comfort" Job (2:11). By "the comforts of God" Eliphaz most likely means the gentle words of his first speech: the vision that came to him in the night (4:12–21) and the promise that God wounds and heals (5:17–26). He presents them as God's own word, spoken gently. Job will answer that they are "comforters who bring trouble" (16:2), and he asks in 21:2 that listening be their only comfort. The book's last word on the friends' comfort comes in 42:7, where God says they have not spoken rightly of him.

a: How can one born of woman be in the right?
p: Eliphaz repeats the message of his night vision (4:17–19) and turns Job's own words, 'born of woman' (14:1), against him.
b: This is the core of Eliphaz's theology, said for the second time: no human can be pure before God, since even heavenly beings fall short (4:17–19). Bildad repeats it once more in 25:4–6. The phrase "born of woman" echoes Job's own lament that a human born of woman has few days and much trouble (14:1). Job used it to plead for pity; Eliphaz uses it to prove guilt. The point is true as far as it goes (Psalm 143:2; Ecclesiastes 7:20), and Job agrees with it in 9:2. The question is whether it explains Job's suffering.

a: a man who gulps down wrong like water
p: A picture of someone who does wrong as easily and often as he drinks. Elihu uses it of Job himself in 34:7.
b: In a dry land, water is drunk freely and without thought. The image is of evil done the same way, by habit and with pleasure. Eliphaz speaks of humans in general, but the line comes close to Job. Elihu will apply the same picture to Job directly, as a man who drinks scorn like water (34:7). Proverbs has a similar picture of a wicked person who "eats" violence and "drinks" wrong (Proverbs 4:17; 19:28).

a: The land was handed to them alone
p: Eliphaz claims his teaching comes from ancestors who lived untouched by foreigners, so it is pure.
b: Eliphaz grounds his teaching in old tradition, not only in his vision (4:12–16): wise men received it from their fathers in a land no outsider (zar) walked through. Teman in Edom was famous for its wise men (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8–9), so the claim fits his name. Scholars disagree on what lies behind the line. Some hear a memory of a golden age before foreign invasion; some, a claim that the tradition was never mixed with foreign ideas; some critical scholars hear a concern for purity common in the Persian period, after the exile. Whatever the setting, the claim is that the tradition is old, native and unmixed, and so can be trusted.

a: The wicked man twists in pain all his days
p: The verb is the one used for a woman in labor, and for Job's being 'birthed' in 15:7. Eliphaz's speech is full of birth language.
b: Mitcholel is from chul, "to writhe", used of labor pains (Isaiah 26:17; Psalm 48:6). The same root gave "birthed" in 15:7. The speech ends with the godless "pregnant with mischief" giving birth to wickedness (15:35). So Eliphaz frames his poem with birth: Job is not the first-born sage; the wicked man lives in a lifelong labor; and his only offspring is evil. The second line, "the counted years", means few years; others read it as "all the years stored up" for the tyrant, a life of dread from start to end.

a: He has no faith that he will come back from the dark
p: Eliphaz's wicked man is tormented by fear even while he prospers.
b: This part of the speech (15:20–24) is about the inner life of the wicked. Even in good times he hears noises in the dark and waits for the sword. Eliphaz is answering Job's claim that the wicked are untroubled (12:6). His view is not foolish; Proverbs says the same, "The wicked flee with no one after them" (Proverbs 28:1). But it is also, in a way, Job's own experience: Job had said that the thing he dreaded had come upon him (3:25). Job will reply in 21:7–13 that many wicked people live and die without any such fear.

a: For he lifted his hand against God
p: Eliphaz draws the wicked man as a soldier charging God. Job will draw God as a soldier charging him (16:14).
b: The picture in 15:25–26 is of a warrior raising his arm against God (El), playing the hero (yitgabbar) against the Almighty (Shaddai), and charging with neck stiff behind his shield. The thick "bosses" are the metal knobs in the middle of a round shield. Eliphaz does not say Job is that man, but the description follows directly on his complaint that Job turns his spirit against God (15:13). In the next chapter Job turns the image around: it is God who "charges me like a fighting man" (16:14).

a: His face is wrapped in his own fat
p: Fat stands for wealth and for a heart grown dull and proud.
b: In the Bible, growing fat often goes with forgetting God: "Jeshurun grew fat, and he kicked" (Deuteronomy 32:15), and of the proud, "their eye looks out from fat" (Psalm 73:7). A "fat heart" is one that no longer feels (Psalm 119:70; Isaiah 6:10). Eliphaz's wicked man is well fed and pleased with himself. The picture contrasts sharply with Job, whose "wasted body" (16:8) and clinging bones (19:20) are what the friends see.

a: He settled in towns that were wiped out
p: Either the wicked man ends up living in ruins, or he dared to rebuild a town under a curse.
b: Two readings are common. On one, this is part of his punishment: the tyrant ends up camping in abandoned towns, in houses fit only to become rubble. On the other, the verse is about his crime: he rebuilt and lived in cities that God had destroyed and that were not to be lived in, as Joshua cursed whoever would rebuild Jericho (Joshua 6:26; 1 Kings 16:34). The Hebrew allows either, and the tense of the verbs is unclear. Either way, he has made his home where God's judgment once fell.

a: his holdings will not reach across the land
p: The word translated 'holdings' occurs only here, and no one is sure what it means. The Greek has 'shadow'.
b: Minlam is found nowhere else in Hebrew. The Plain follows the common guess from context, "what they own". The Vulgate's radicem, "root", points rather toward a plant picture. The Greek translator read something like "he will not cast a shadow on the earth" (Rahlfs 15:29), perhaps from a slightly different Hebrew text. Others divide or correct the letters to get "their grain" or "his ears of grain bending to the ground", which fits the plant pictures that follow. The general sense, that his wealth will not last or spread, is clear; the image is not.

a: and he will be blown off by the breath of his mouth
p: 'His mouth' is probably God's mouth, though God is not named. The Greek reads 'his blossom will fall'.
b: The Hebrew says only "by the breath of his mouth". Most interpreters take it as God's breath, which destroys the wicked as in Isaiah 11:4 ("the breath of his lips will put the wicked to death") and 4:9 ("by the breath of God they perish"). The Greek has "may his blossom fall", which suggests a Hebrew text with pircho ("his blossom") rather than piv ("his mouth"), and many scholars think that reading fits the plant picture better. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.
orig: בְּרוּחַ פִּיו (beruach piv), 'by the breath of his mouth'

a: He will lose his green grapes the way a vine does
p: The wicked man is like a plant that loses its fruit and flowers before harvest.
b: Eliphaz ends with pictures from farming: a palm frond that will not turn green (15:32), a vine that drops its grapes while still sour, an olive tree that sheds its blossoms. An olive tree does lose most of its flowers, which may be part of the point: what looks like promise comes to nothing. The wicked may flourish for a time, but they do not last until harvest. The image answers Job's picture of the tree that has hope (14:7–9) and anticipates Bildad's withered roots and branches (18:16).

a: fire will eat the tents built on bribes
p: Fire from God and bribery: both point, without naming him, toward Job's own story.
b: The "tents of bribery" are homes bought with corrupt judgments, since leading men sat as judges at the town gate (29:7). The Greek has "death is the witness of the ungodly" in the first line. Eliphaz does not name Job, but his hearers know that "the fire of God" fell from the sky and burned Job's flocks (1:16) and that Job has lost his children. In his third speech Eliphaz will drop the hints and accuse Job of exact crimes against the poor (22:5–9), which Job denies under oath (29:11–17; 31:13–22).

a: Pregnant with mischief, they give birth to wickedness
p: A proverb also found in Psalm 7 and Isaiah 59: evil is conceived, carried and born.
b: The saying uses three words for evil: 'amal (trouble, mischief), aven (wickedness) and mirmah (deceit). Psalm 7:14 says the wicked man "conceives trouble, and what he bears is a lie", and Isaiah 59:4 has "they conceive trouble and give birth to wickedness". James uses the same picture: desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin gives birth to death (James 1:15). Eliphaz said in his first speech that those who plow wickedness and sow trouble reap them (4:8).

a: You are all comforters who bring trouble!
p: Literally 'comforters of trouble': the friends came to comfort, and their comfort has become one more trouble.
b: Menachame 'amal is a sharp phrase. The friends came to sympathize with him and comfort him (2:11), using the verb nacham. Job now says their comfort is made of 'amal, the very "trouble" that Eliphaz said the wicked conceive (15:35) and that Job said fills human life (3:10; 7:3). The English phrase "Job's comforters", for people who make things worse while trying to help, comes from this verse and the book as a whole.

a: Will words of wind ever stop?
p: Job hands Eliphaz's insult (15:2) straight back to him.
b: Eliphaz opened by asking whether a wise man answers with knowledge that is only wind (15:2). Job answers with the same word, ruach: it is the friends' words that are wind. The second line, "What is bothering you?", is singular in Hebrew, aimed at Eliphaz, while the rest of the chapter speaks to all three friends in the plural. The Old Greek lacked part of this verse; Origen supplied the missing words from Theodotion.

a: and wag my head at you
p: The head-shake was a gesture of scorn. A similar word in 16:5 and 2:11 means sympathy. Job plays on both.
b: To shake or wag the head (heni'a berosh) at someone is a gesture of mockery: "All who see me make fun of me... they sneer with their lips and shake their heads" (Psalm 22:7); passers-by "wag their heads" at ruined Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:15) and at Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:39; Mark 15:29). In 16:5 Job uses a related word, nid, "moving" of the lips, and the friends had come "to nod" with him, lanud, meaning to show sympathy (2:11). The gesture of comfort and the gesture of scorn sit side by side. Job says that if their places were changed, he could mock them, or he could really comfort them, as they have not.

a: I would make you strong with my mouth
p: Job may mean he would truly comfort them, or he may be mocking their 'strengthening' words.
b: Read straight, 16:5 contrasts what Job would do with what the friends have done: he would strengthen them with real comfort (compare 4:3–4, where Eliphaz praises Job for strengthening the weak). Read as irony, it continues 16:4: "I could pile up words like you, and strengthen you with mere mouth-comfort, the kind that moves only the lips." Both readings have able defenders among commentators. Either way, 16:6 adds that words, his or theirs, do not touch his pain.

a: You have wrecked my whole circle.
p: Job speaks about God and then to God in the same breath. 'My circle' may be his household, now destroyed.
b: The verse moves from "he" to "you" without warning, and so does the passage that follows (16:7–8 "you", 16:9–14 "he"). This is common in laments, where the sufferer turns from describing God to addressing him (Psalm 23:1–4). Some translators supply "God" or "O God"; the Plain keeps the Hebrew pronouns. 'Edah, "circle" or "company", usually means a community or gathering. Here it most likely means Job's household, his children and servants who died in 1:13–19; some take it as his circle of friends, who now stand against him (16:20; 19:13–19).

a: You have gripped me, and that has become a witness.
p: Job's illness is treated as testimony against him: everyone, the friends included, reads his sores as proof of guilt.
b: The verb qamat means to seize (22:16 has the wicked "snatched away"), and some render it "you have shriveled me". Either way, the result "has become a witness". Job's wasted body (kachash, leanness; the word can also mean "lie, deception", which is how the Greek took it) stands up in court and speaks against him. This is the logic of the friends' theology: if God has struck him, he must be guilty, so his suffering itself is evidence. Job has begun to think in terms of a trial (9:2–3; 13:18), and the courtroom picture grows through this chapter to the witness in heaven (16:19).
orig: וַתִּקְמְטֵנִי לְעֵד הָיָה (vattiqmeteni le'ed hayah), 'you seized me; it became a witness'

a: he holds a grudge against me
p: The verb satam, 'bear a grudge', is a close cousin of satan, 'accuse, oppose'. Job blames God for what the reader knows the Accuser began.
b: Satam means to hate and hold a grudge, as Esau did against Jacob (Genesis 27:41) and as Joseph's brothers feared he would (Genesis 50:15). It is closely related to satan, "to oppose, accuse", which gives the title of the Accuser in 1:6–12 and 2:1–7. Job uses it again in 30:21, of God's strong hand holding a grudge against him. The reader knows something Job does not. The Accuser proposed the test, though God allowed it (2:3). Job, who knows nothing of the heavenly scene, gives God the Accuser's role, calling him "my foe" (tsari) who glares at him.
orig: וַיִּשְׂטְמֵנִי (vayyistemeni), 'and he bore a grudge against me'

a: They hit me on the cheek to shame me.
p: A slap on the cheek was a public insult. Christians have heard in Job's mockers the mocking of Jesus.
b: To strike someone on the cheek was to shame them in public (1 Kings 22:24; Lamentations 3:30; Micah 5:1). The suffering servant gives his cheeks to those who pull out his beard (Isaiah 50:6), and in the Gospels the guards strike Jesus (Matthew 26:67; John 18:22). From the early church on, Christian readers saw in Job, mocked, struck and handed over to the wicked by God (16:11), a picture of Christ in his passion. Gregory the Great reads the whole book that way, with Job as a figure of Christ and of the church. The text itself speaks only of Job.
r: 1 Kings 22:24; Lamentations 3:30; Micah 5:1; Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 26:67; John 18:22; 30:9–10

a: God delivers me to the unjust
p: The word 'avil may mean 'an unjust one' or, with different vowels, 'a boy'. Either way, God hands Job over to his worst.
b: The Hebrew 'avil is rare. Most take it as a form of 'avval, "unjust person", matching "the wicked" in the second line. With other vowels the same letters give 'awil, "young boy", the word in 19:18 and 21:11, and some versions have "the young": Job is handed over to youths who mock him (compare 30:1–12). The Plain follows the parallel with "the wicked". The striking claim is the subject of the verb: it is God (El) who hands him over.

a: He stood me up as a target for himself.
p: Job pictures God as a wrestler, an archer and a soldier breaching a city wall.
b: In 16:12–14 Job uses three pictures of violence. God grabs him by the neck like a wrestler; sets him up as a target and lets his archers shoot (compare 6:4, where the Almighty's arrows are in him); and breaks through him "gap on top of gap", as an army breaks through a city wall. Lamentations uses the same words of God against Jerusalem: he bent his bow and set me as a target for the arrow (Lamentations 3:12–13). For readers who knew Jerusalem's fall, Job's body had become a city under siege. Compare the siege in 19:12.

a: He slices my kidneys open without mercy
p: Kidneys and gall were thought of as the deepest, most vital parts. Spilling them means a death wound.
b: In Hebrew thought the kidneys (kelayot) were the seat of the deepest feelings and conscience; God "tests hearts and kidneys" (Psalm 7:9; compare Jeremiah 11:20), and Job's inmost being (his kidneys) is spent with longing in 19:27. The gall or bile (merorah) was a vital organ; a wound that spilled it was fatal. Zophar uses the same word when the arrow comes out of the wicked man's "gallbladder" (20:25). Job is describing a wound no one survives.

a: I have thrust my horn into the dust.
p: The horn stands for strength and honor. Job has buried it, as a mourner sits in dust.
b: An animal's horn is its strength and pride, so in Hebrew "to lift up the horn" means to be strong or honored (1 Samuel 2:1; Psalm 75:4–5; Psalm 89:17). To thrust it into the dust is the opposite: complete humiliation. Sackcloth, coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning, is usually put on; Job says he has "stitched" it on, as if he will never take it off. Dust was thrown on the head in grief (2:12), and Job sat in ashes (2:8). In 42:6 he speaks of "dust and ashes" again.
orig: וְעֹלַלְתִּי בֶעָפָר קַרְנִי (ve'olalti ve'afar qarni), 'I have thrust my horn in the dust'

a: deep shadow lies on my eyelids
p: Tsalmavet is either 'deep darkness' or, as the Masoretes divided it, 'shadow of death'.
b: The word tsalmavet appears ten times in Job (3:5; 10:21–22; 12:22; 24:17; 28:3; 34:22; 38:17) and elsewhere, most famously in Psalm 23:4. The Masoretic vowels treat it as two words, tsel mavet, "shadow of death", and the Greek and the KJV follow that. Many scholars think it is one word meaning "deep darkness", from a root "to be dark". The Plain has "deep shadow" here, as everywhere in Job, and leaves "shadow of death" to this note. Here the darkness is on Job's eyelids: the dark rings of a man worn out with crying, and a sign that death is near.

a: This, though my hands have done no violence
p: Job's claim matches what Isaiah says of the suffering servant: he had done no violence.
b: "No violence" (lo chamas) is the same phrase used of the servant of the LORD in Isaiah 53:9, who suffered though "he had done no violence". David protests the same way to Saul's men (1 Chronicles 12:17). Job's "clean" prayer is a prayer from clean hands (compare Psalm 24:4; Psalm 66:18). This is the claim the whole debate turns on. The friends assume that suffering proves guilt; Job insists that in his case it does not, and the reader knows from 1:1 and 1:8 that he is right.

a: Earth, do not hide my blood!
p: Job asks the earth to keep his blood uncovered, so that it keeps crying for justice, like Abel's.
b: In Israel's thinking, the blood of a murdered person cried out from the ground until justice was done: "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Covering blood with dust silenced it (Ezekiel 24:7–8), and on the day of judgment "the earth will lay bare its blood" (Isaiah 26:21). Job treats his coming death as a murder and asks the earth not to bury the case. His "outcry" (za'aqah) is a legal cry for help. The verse leads straight into 16:19: if the earth keeps his cry alive, someone in heaven must hear it. Hebrews 12:24 contrasts Abel's blood with the blood of Jesus, "which speaks better".

a: my witness is in heaven
p: Job uses the Hebrew 'ed and its Aramaic twin sahed. The second is the word in Laban's 'heap of witness'.
b: 'Ed is the ordinary Hebrew word for a witness. Sahed, "the one who vouches for me", is its Aramaic equivalent, found only here in the Hebrew Bible, though Laban's Aramaic name for the heap of stones, Jegar-sahadutha, "heap of witness", uses the same root (Genesis 31:47). Pairing a common word with a rare or foreign one is typical of the poet of Job. In Israel a witness did more than report facts: he took a side in court and could defend the accused (Deuteronomy 19:15–19; Isaiah 43:9–10). On who this witness might be, see the next note.
orig: עֵדִי ('edi), 'my witness'; שָׂהֲדִי (sahadi), 'my one who testifies' (Aramaic)

a: Even now, look: my witness is in heaven
t: Who is the witness in heaven?
p: God himself, a heavenly figure who will take Job's side against God, Job's own cry, or Christ: all four have strong defenders.
b: Job has wished for an umpire between himself and God (9:33). Now he says that his witness already exists, "in heaven". Who? God himself: the God Job knows will testify against the God who attacks him, an appeal from God to God (Gordis, Andersen, Hartley). A heavenly figure other than God: a member of the divine council, a counter-Accuser who will plead for Job, like the "mediating angel" of 33:23 (Mowinckel, Pope, Habel, Newsom). Job's own cry: his outcry of 16:18, which rises to heaven and testifies for him (Clines). Christ: Christian readers from Gregory the Great onward saw the advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1; Hebrews 7:25). The same question returns at 19:25.

a: The ones who mock me are my friends!
p: The Hebrew can mean 'my scorners' or 'my spokesmen'. Some read 'my spokesman is my friend', meaning the witness of 16:19.
b: Melitsay comes from lits, which gives both "scoffer" (Proverbs 1:22) and melits, an interpreter or go-between (Genesis 42:23; Isaiah 43:27), the "mediating angel" of 33:23. As vowelled, it is plural, "my scorners are my friends", a bitter cry about Eliphaz and company; the Plain follows that. Many modern scholars read the singular melitsi, "my spokesman is my friend", which continues 16:19: the heavenly witness speaks for Job while Job weeps toward God. The Greek has neither: "may my prayer come to the Lord". The ambiguity may be deliberate, setting the false friends on earth beside the true friend in heaven.
orig: מְלִיצַי רֵעָי (melitsay re'ay), 'my scorners/interpreters are my friends'

a: May he plead for a man before God
t: A son of man for his friend
p: The witness pleads with God as one person pleads for a friend. The Hebrew 'son of man' has drawn Christian readers.
b: The verb yokhach is legal: to argue a case, to decide between parties (9:33 uses it of the umpire). The witness argues for Job "with God", so the witness and God are distinct in the picture, whatever lies behind it. The second line literally says "and a son of man (ben adam) for his friend". Many scholars read uven ("and between"): "as between a man and his friend". The Plain renders ben adam as "a mortal". Christian readers have heard here a mediator who is both on God's side and a son of man (1 Timothy 2:5); the Greek has "and a son of man for his neighbor".
orig: וְיוֹכַח לְגֶבֶר עִם־אֱלוֹהַּ וּבֶן־אָדָם לְרֵעֵהוּ (veyokhach legever 'im-Eloah uven-adam lere'ehu)

a: and I will walk a road I do not come back on
p: Job expects to die before any vindication comes, which makes the hope of 16:19 and 19:25 all the more striking.
b: Death as a journey from which no one returns is a common picture in Job (7:9–10; 10:21) and elsewhere in the Bible (2 Samuel 12:23). In Mesopotamian poems the underworld is "the land of no return". Job's hope of a witness is not a hope of recovery: he expects to die soon (17:1). That is why interpreters ask whether the vindication he hopes for in 19:25–27 comes before death, after it, or in a way he cannot picture.

a: Graves are what is left for me.
p: Job's days are 'snuffed out' like a lamp, using a rare verb, and 'graves' is plural, like a cemetery waiting.
b: Niz'akhu, "they are snuffed out", occurs only here; it is related to an Aramaic verb for putting out a flame, and it picks up the lamp of life that the friends say goes out for the wicked (18:5–6; 21:17). "Graves" is plural, perhaps meaning a burial ground, or simply "the grave" in a strong form. Chapter 17 continues Job's speech without a break; the chapter division here, made in the Middle Ages, falls in the middle of the thought.
orig: יָמַי נִזְעָכוּ קְבָרִים לִי (yamay niz'akhu qevarim li), 'my days are snuffed out; graves are mine'

a: and my eye spends the night on their taunts
p: The verb lun means 'to stay the night'. Job lies awake with the friends' taunts in front of him.
b: Talan is from lun, to lodge or spend the night (Genesis 19:2; Ruth 3:13). Job's eye "spends the night" on the provocations of his mockers: he cannot stop seeing them. The same verb comes in 19:4, where Job says his error "lodges" with him. The first line, "truly mockery is all I have around me", uses an oath form (im lo, "surely").

a: stand bail for me with yourself
p: Job asks God to put up the bail for Job's case before God. No one else will strike hands for him.
b: To "strike hands" was to seal a pledge as someone's guarantor, promising to pay if they could not (Proverbs 6:1; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 22:26). Judah stood surety for Benjamin (Genesis 43:9; Genesis 44:32). Job asks God to "set down" a deposit and be his guarantor "with yourself": in a case between Job and God, God is asked to pledge for Job to God. It is the same paradox as the witness in heaven (16:19–21) and the redeemer (19:25): Job appeals to God against God, because there is no one else. Psalm 119:122 prays the same: "Stand surety for your servant, for his good." The Greek of 17:2–3 reads quite differently, of strangers who have stolen Job's goods.
orig: עָרְבֵנִי עִמָּךְ ('orveni 'immakh), 'be my guarantor with yourself'
r: 16:19–21; 19:25; Proverbs 6:1; Proverbs 17:18; Genesis 43:9; Genesis 44:32; Psalm 119:122; Isaiah 38:14; Hebrews 7:22

a: Whoever betrays his friends for a cut of the profit
p: The line is probably a proverb, but its meaning is unclear: betraying friends for gain, or feasting friends while one's children starve.
b: Literally: "for a share he tells friends, and the eyes of his children fail". The Plain takes yaggid, "he tells", as informing against friends for a share of the gain, and the second line as the punishment that falls on his children (compare 5:4; 20:10). A second reading takes it as a proverb about foolish generosity: "He invites friends to share his goods, while his own children's eyes fail with hunger", that is, the friends are generous with words while Job wastes away. A third sees the friends themselves, who speak of Job's "share" from God (20:29) while Job's family is gone. The short line allows all three.

a: I am a face for spitting in.
t: A byword and a face to spit on
p: God has made Job a proverb among the nations, the fate Deuteronomy threatens for an unfaithful Israel.
b: To become a mashal, a proverb or "byword", is the curse of Deuteronomy 28:37 and 1 Kings 9:7: people point to you as the example of disaster. Spitting in the face is the deepest insult (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9; Isaiah 50:6), and Job says it happens to him in 30:10. The rare word tofet, "spitting", is spelled like Topheth, the place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), and a few interpreters have seen a pun. For readers in or after the exile, Job's fate looked like Israel's own: a byword among the peoples, though Job, unlike the Israel of Deuteronomy 28, has not been unfaithful.
r: Deuteronomy 28:37; 1 Kings 9:7; Psalm 44:14; 30:9–10; Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9; Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 26:67

a: Honest men are stunned by this
t: Job's faith, or the friends' slogan?
p: Job may be voicing his own conviction that the righteous will hold out, or mocking what the friends say.
b: 17:8–9 seems out of place in Job's despair: the upright are shocked at the godless, and "the righteous man keeps on his road". Three readings are held. Job's own faith: even now he believes integrity is worth keeping, and he himself will "keep on his road" (compare 23:11; 27:6); Christian preachers have long used 17:9 as a text on perseverance. Irony: Job quotes the friends' kind of maxim, then dismisses it in 17:10, "I will not find one wise man among you". A misplaced line: some critics move the verses to a friend's speech. The Plain translates the lines as they stand.

a: They call night day.
p: The friends promise light to a man in darkness. Zophar had said that Job's darkness would become like morning (11:17).
b: "They" are most likely the friends, whose advice turns night into day: they keep telling Job that the light is near if he repents. Zophar had promised that Job's life would rise brighter than noon and his darkness be like the morning (11:17), and Eliphaz will promise the same (22:28). Job's "plans" and "wishes" (17:11) are gone, and their cheerful promises cannot change that. Isaiah condemns those who "make dark into light and light into dark" (Isaiah 5:20), though the situation is different.

a: If all I look forward to is Sheol as my house
t: Sheol as a house with beds
p: Sheol, the realm of the dead, is pictured as a dark house where the dead lie on beds.
b: Sheol is the Hebrew Bible's name for the realm of the dead, deep below the earth. Job calls it the meeting house of all the living (30:23), and here pictures it as a home where he will make his bed in the dark. Isaiah pictures maggots as the bed and worms as the blanket of the dead king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:11), and Ezekiel the slain lying on beds in the pit (Ezekiel 32:25). Graves in Job's world were often family tombs cut in rock, with benches on which bodies were laid, so the picture of a bed was close to life.

a: if I call the Pit "my father"
t: A new family in the grave
p: Abandoned by his living family, Job imagines calling the grave his father and the maggot his mother and sister.
b: Shachat means the pit, the grave, and in later Hebrew "corruption, decay". The Greek has "death" and "decay" here, and the Greek of Psalm 16:10 has "corruption" for the same word, a verse that Acts 2:27 applies to Jesus' resurrection. Job speaks the language of kinship: "father", "mother", "sister". His brothers and friends have abandoned him (19:13–19), so the grave and its maggots will be his family. The image prepares for the go'el of 19:25, the family member whose duty is to rescue his kin.
orig: לַשַּׁחַת קָרָאתִי אָבִי אָתָּה (lashachat qarati avi attah), 'to the pit I cried, You are my father'

a: and the maggot "my mother" and "my sister,"
p: The oldest surviving translation of Job, an Aramaic scroll from Qumran Cave 11, begins around here.
b: 11QtgJob (also called 11Q10) is an Aramaic translation of Job copied in the first century BC or the first century AD and found in Cave 11 at Qumran in 1956. It is the oldest surviving translation of Job besides the Greek. What is left begins with scraps of 17:14–16 and 18:1–4 and continues, with gaps, to 42:11, where it ends. In chapters 17–21 the published editions report columns covering about 17:14–18:4, 19:11–19, 19:29–20:6, 21:2–10 and 21:20–27. It is not a word-for-word copy of the Masoretic Text, and it is unrelated to the later rabbinic Targum of Job. I checked these ranges against reports of the editions, not the plates.

a: Will they sink to the bars of Sheol?
p: Job's hopes go down with him into Sheol, pictured as a city or prison with barred gates.
b: "They" are Job's hopes (17:15); the Greek has "my good things". Badde usually means "poles, bars", the bars of a gate (compare Jonah 2:6, "the earth with its bars"), so Sheol is a prison with locked gates (compare 38:17, "the gates of death"). The Greek reads "will they go down with me ('immadi) to Hades?", which fits the second line, "side by side". Either way, Job's hope dies with him. This is the low point from which 19:25 will rise.
orig: בַּדֵּי שְׁאֹל (badde she'ol), 'the bars of Sheol'

a: How long before you put a stop to words?
p: Bildad's word qintse is unique. It may mean 'ends' or 'snares', and 'you' is plural.
b: Qintse occurs only here. Most link it with qets, "end" (an Aramaic-style plural): "How long until you make an end of words?" Others connect it with an Arabic and Akkadian root for hunting: "How long will you set snares of words?", which would fit the hunting pictures of 18:8–10. Oddly, "you" in 18:2–3 is plural, though Bildad speaks to Job. He may be lumping Job with people like him, or answering Job's attack on all three friends (16:2; 17:10). Bildad opened his first speech the same way, asking how long Job would talk like this (8:2).
orig: קִנְצֵי לְמִלִּין (qintse lemillin), 'ends (or snares) for words'

a: Why do you treat us like dumb animals?
p: Job had told the friends to go and learn from the animals (12:7). Bildad takes offense.
b: Job had said: ask the animals and the birds, and they will teach you that God's hand does this (12:7–9), and that his friends had no understanding (17:4, 10). Bildad hears this as being called a beast. The verb nitminu is probably "we are thought stupid" (from tamam, "to be stopped up"), though the Vulgate and some later readers took it as "unclean" (tame'). The irony is that the animals will in fact be God's teaching tools in chapters 38–41.

a: You, ripping yourself apart in your rage
p: Job said God's anger tore him (16:9). Bildad says Job is tearing himself, and the world will not change for him.
b: In 16:9 Job said, "His anger rips me apart." Bildad answers with the same verb, taraf: it is Job's own anger that tears him. His questions turn another of Job's pictures around: Job had lamented that God wears away hope as water wears away stone and shifts a rock out of its place (14:18). Bildad says the moral order of the world, as solid as rock, will not be rearranged to suit one complaining man. This is the heart of his position, and a strong one: the rules that govern the world cannot bend for each case.

a: Still, the wicked man's light is snuffed
p: A lamp burning in the tent meant a living household. Its going out meant death and the end of the family line.
b: A small clay lamp was kept burning in a home through the night; a dark house was a dead or empty one (Jeremiah 25:10). So "lamp" stands for life and for a family's survival: "the lamp of the wicked will be put out" (Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 24:20), while God promises David "a lamp" in Jerusalem, meaning a continuing line (1 Kings 11:36; 2 Kings 8:19). Bildad uses the picture of every family that perishes, and Job's own house has gone dark (1:18–19). Job will answer with a direct question: "How many times does the wicked man's lamp go dark?" (21:17).
r: 21:17; Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 24:20; Proverbs 20:20; Jeremiah 25:10; 1 Kings 11:36; 2 Kings 8:19; 29:3

a: His own feet send him into a net
p: Bildad uses six different Hebrew words for nets and snares in three verses: the wicked walk into traps they cannot see.
b: In 18:8–10 Bildad piles up the vocabulary of the hunter: reshet (net), sevakhah (netting, lattice), pach (spring-trap), tsammim (noose or snare), chevel (cord, rope) and malkodet (trap). Nets for birds and pits and nooses for animals are well known from ancient art; Egyptian tomb paintings show clap-nets for birds. The point is that the wicked trap themselves: "his own feet" lead him in (compare Psalm 9:15; Proverbs 5:22). Job will reply that it is God who has thrown the net over him (19:6).
r: 19:6; Psalm 9:15; Psalm 91:3; Proverbs 5:22; Amos 3:5; Hosea 7:12; Ecclesiastes 9:12

a: Death's firstborn feeds on his limbs
p: Probably the worst disease, Death's eldest son. In Canaanite myth Death (Mot) is a god with a huge appetite.
b: "Firstborn" can mean the chief or strongest of a group (Isaiah 14:30, "the firstborn of the poor" means the poorest). "Death's firstborn" is most likely a deadly disease, the worst that Death sends. In the Ugaritic myths from Syria (about 1300 BC), Mot ("Death") is a god who swallows his victims with an enormous throat, and some scholars think Bildad borrows that picture: Death and his offspring eat the wicked. The poet need not believe in Mot to use the image, just as Isaiah pictures Sheol opening its mouth (Isaiah 5:14). Bildad's description of skin being eaten away also fits Job's own disease (2:7–8; 7:5), which makes it a cruel hint.
orig: בְּכוֹר מָוֶת (bekhor mavet), 'the firstborn of death'

a: and paraded before the king of terrors
p: Death or the lord of the dead, pictured as a king to whom the wicked are marched as captives.
b: The wicked man is torn from his tent and marched, like a prisoner of war, to "the king of terrors", which is Death personified. The Mesopotamians had a king of the underworld, Nergal, with his queen Ereshkigal, and Ugaritic texts picture Mot enthroned in his city below. Israel did not worship such a god, but its poets could speak of death as a ruler (Psalm 49:14, "Death will shepherd them"; Hosea 13:14; Isaiah 28:15). The New Testament takes up the same picture when it calls death the last enemy to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26) and says Christ freed those held in slavery by fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).
r: 18:11; 18:13; Psalm 49:14; Hosea 13:14; Isaiah 28:15; 1 Corinthians 15:26; Hebrews 2:14–15; Revelation 6:8

a: Something not his settles in his tent
t: What lives in the empty tent?
p: The Hebrew 'what is not his' is unclear: strangers, wild animals, or (with a small change) fire. Sulfur recalls Sodom.
b: Mibbeli-lo, "from not-his", is hard. It may mean that strangers move into the dead man's tent; or that it becomes a home for "what is not his", wild animals and spirits of the desert (compare Isaiah 34:11–15); or, with a small change of letters, that "fire" lives in his tent, which matches the sulfur of the second line. Sulfur (gofrit) recalls Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24; Deuteronomy 29:23; Psalm 11:6). For Job's hearers, "fire" falling on a man's property recalls 1:16, where "the fire of God" burned up his sheep.

a: No one in the land remembers him anymore
p: In Israel a person lived on through his name, carried by his children. To lose it was the final ruin.
b: Survival of one's name mattered deeply: the law of levirate marriage existed so that a dead man's "name will not be wiped out from Israel" (Deuteronomy 25:6), and childless Absalom set up a pillar to keep his name (2 Samuel 18:18). Bildad's picture of the wicked man, with no memory, no name in the street and no descendants (18:19), describes exactly what has happened to Job, whose ten children are dead (1:18–19). Isaiah later promises the faithful eunuch a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:5).

a: He leaves no child or grandchild among his people
p: A rhyming pair of rare words for descendants, used again only in Genesis 21:23 and Isaiah 14:22.
b: Nin va-neked, "offspring and offspring's offspring", is a fixed pair, like English "kith and kin". Abimelech asks Abraham not to deal falsely with him or his nin and neked (Genesis 21:23), and God promises to cut off Babylon's nin and neked (Isaiah 14:22). Job's answer comes in 21:8: the wicked he has seen have children established around them. In the book's ending, Job himself will see his children's children to four generations (42:16).

a: Those who come after are stunned by his day
t: West and east, or later and earlier?
p: The two words mean 'the ones behind' and 'the ones in front'. That is either later and earlier people, or the west and the east.
b: Acharonim and qadmonim usually mean "later ones" and "former ones" (Ecclesiastes 1:11), and the KJV has "they that come after him... they that went before". But since Hebrew speakers faced east when giving directions, "behind" is west and "in front" is east (Zechariah 14:8; Joel 2:20), and most modern translations read "those in the west... those in the east": the whole world is horrified at the wicked man's fate. The Plain keeps the literal sense and leaves this note for the second reading. "His day" means the day of his downfall (compare Psalm 37:13).
orig: אַחֲרֹנִים / קַדְמֹנִים (acharonim / qadmonim), 'those behind / those in front'

a: that is the place of one who does not know God
p: Bildad ends with a summary that fits Job's losses point by point. The implication is plain: Job does not know God.
b: To "know God" in the Hebrew Bible means more than to know about him: it is loyal relationship and obedience (Jeremiah 22:16; Hosea 4:1, 6). Bildad never names Job, but every disaster he lists matches Job's life: fire on his property, a house without children, skin eaten away, friends and townspeople horrified. A fair reading of Bildad notes that he is defending something precious, a world where evil does not win; the Psalms say much the same (Psalm 37). But the book has told the reader that Job is the one person on earth who fears God most (1:8), and God's verdict on the friends in 42:7 rejects the use they make of the doctrine.

a: How long will you grieve my soul
p: Job answers Bildad's 'How long?' (18:2) with his own.
b: Bildad began, "How long before you put a stop to words?" (18:2; compare 8:2). Job turns the question back. The verb yagah, "grieve, torment", is used in Lamentations of God afflicting Jerusalem (Lamentations 1:5, 12; Lamentations 3:32–33). "How long?" is the typical cry of the lament psalms (Psalm 13:1–2), but here it is aimed at friends, not at God.

a: This is the tenth time you have shamed me.
t: Ten times, and a rare verb
p: 'Ten times' means 'over and over'. The verb for 'abuse' is found only here.
b: "Ten times" is a round number for "again and again", as when Jacob says Laban changed his wages ten times (Genesis 31:7) or God says Israel tested him ten times (Numbers 14:22). The verb tahkeru, "you abuse me", occurs only here. It is usually linked with an Arabic word meaning "to wrong, ill-treat"; others propose "to stun" or "to be hard on". The sense is clear from the context: the friends have humiliated him without shame.

a: My mistake is my own to keep.
p: Job does not admit guilt; he says that even an unknowing slip would be his own affair, not a reason for their attacks.
b: Shagah means to err without intent, the kind of sin for which the Law provides an offering (Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:27–28). Job is not confessing. He grants for argument's sake that he may have slipped without knowing it, and says it "lodges" with him (talin, the verb of 17:2): it is between him and God, and harms no one else. It could not justify what has been done to him. The Greek adds a line here, discussed in the variants.

a: it is God who has bent my case
p: Job uses the very verb of Bildad's question 'Does God bend justice?' (8:3), and answers yes.
b: In his first speech Bildad asked whether God bends justice or the Almighty bends what is right (8:3), using 'ivvet, "to make crooked, falsify". Job now says exactly that: God has "bent" him, put him in the wrong. It is the boldest charge in the book so far. Ecclesiastes uses the same verb: "Who is able to set straight what he has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13). The second line answers Bildad again: the wicked walk into their own net (18:8), says Bildad; God has thrown his net over me, says Job.

a: If I scream "Violence!" no one answers me.
p: 'Chamas!' was the cry of someone being attacked, calling on anyone in earshot, and on the court, to help.
b: Crying "Violence!" (chamas) was a legal act: a victim called out for help, and anyone who heard was bound to come (compare Deuteronomy 22:24, 27, where the woman who "cries out" in the field is presumed innocent). Habakkuk prays, "LORD, how long have I been crying for help, with you not listening? I shout to you, 'Violence!' and still you will not save" (Habakkuk 1:2), and Jeremiah says, "I am shouting, 'Violence! Ruin!'" (Jeremiah 20:8). Job's cry gets no answer, because the one attacking him is the judge.

a: He has built a wall across my road; I can't get through.
p: Job 19:7–12 and Lamentations 3:1–9 share words and pictures: walled-in roads, darkness, a God who attacks like an enemy.
b: Lamentations 3 is the lament of "the man who has seen affliction" after Jerusalem's fall: God has driven him into darkness, walled him in so that he cannot get out, shut out his prayer, and blocked his ways with cut stones (Lamentations 3:2, 7–9). Job uses the same verb gadar, "build a wall", and the same darkness, and in 19:10 the same uprooted hope. Scholars debate which text knew the other, or whether both draw on a common language of lament. For readers after 587 BC, Job's personal disaster spoke in the words they used for the national one. Hosea pictures God walling in Israel's way to bring her back (Hosea 2:6).

a: He pulled off the glory I wore
p: Job's honor was like clothing and a crown. God has stripped both away.
b: "Glory" (kavod) means weight, honor, standing in the community. Job will describe that standing in chapter 29: the elders rose when he came to the town gate, and he wore justice like a robe and a turban (29:7–14). Now it is stripped off him like a garment (compare 1:20, where he tore his robe). A crown fallen from the head is the image Lamentations uses for Jerusalem: "The crown of our head has fallen" (Lamentations 5:16). Psalm 8:5 says God crowned humans with glory and honor.

a: he rips my hope up by the roots like a tree
p: Job had said a tree cut down can sprout again (14:7). His own hope is pulled up by the roots.
b: In 14:7–9 Job said there is hope for a tree: cut it down, and at the smell of water it will sprout again. A human, he lamented, has no such second life. Now even that small comparison fails: his hope is not cut down but uprooted. The picture prepares the turn in 19:25. After saying his hope is gone (17:15; 19:10), Job suddenly speaks with certainty: "I know."

a: They pile up a roadway to reach me
p: God's troops build a siege road and camp around Job's tent: a whole army besieging one man's tent.
b: To "pile up a roadway" is siege language: armies built earth ramps up to a city wall, as the Assyrians did at Lachish in 701 BC (2 Kings 19:32; Isaiah 37:33). The gedudim are raiding bands. The picture is exaggerated on purpose: a whole army building ramps against one tent. It shows how out of proportion Job feels God's attack to be. In 16:14 God broke through him like a city wall; here he besieges him. Compare 10:17, where God's "troops" relieve one another against him.

a: My brothers he has moved far away from me
p: Job lists everyone who has abandoned him, moving inward from brothers to servants to wife and children.
b: In 19:13–19 the list runs: brothers, acquaintances, kin, close friends, house guests, slave girls, servant, wife, his own family, even street children, and finally his inner circle. In a society built on family and honor, a man was who his network said he was, so losing them was a social death. Job blames God for it ("he has moved"), as the lament psalms do: "You have taken my friends far from me; you have made me disgusting to them" (Psalm 88:8; compare Psalm 31:11; Psalm 38:11). The list sets up the go'el of 19:25: when every relative has failed, Job looks for the one kinsman who will not.

a: The foreigners who live in my house
t: Guests who treat the master as a stranger
p: The resident foreigners of his own house treat Job as an outsider and a foreigner. Three words for 'stranger' collide.
b: Gare veti are "those who live as ger in my house": dependents, guests or resident foreigners who lived under Job's protection (31:32 says he opened his door to the traveler). Now they treat him as a zar, an outsider, and as a nokhri, a foreigner. The Plain follows the site's usual renderings so the reader can see the reversal: the foreigners in his house have made the master the foreigner. Ruth uses nokhriyyah of herself (Ruth 2:10).
orig: גָּרֵי בֵיתִי (gare veti), 'the sojourners of my house'

a: I am sickening to the sons of my own womb
p: Job's children are dead (1:19), so 'sons of my womb' must mean brothers from his mother's womb, or the line is a bitter cry.
b: Two words are uncertain. Ruchi zarah is either "my breath is repulsive" (from zur, "to be loathsome") or "my spirit is strange" to my wife. Channoti can be "I am loathsome" or "I beg" (from chanan). Then "the sons of my womb": since his sons died in 1:19, most take it as "the sons of my mother's womb", his brothers, since Job calls his mother's womb "my womb" in 3:10. Others think of grandchildren or of children by servant wives. A few think the poet simply uses the cry of every sufferer without fitting it to the frame story.
orig: לִבְנֵי בִטְנִי (livne vitni), 'to the sons of my belly'

a: Even small children reject me
p: In a culture that honored age, being mocked by children was the deepest disgrace.
b: Old age and high standing were honored: young men stepped back and elders stood up when Job passed (29:8). Now small boys ('avilim) jeer at him when he rises. Elisha was mocked by boys at Bethel (2 Kings 2:23), and Isaiah pictures a society falling apart when "Boys will sneer at the old" (Isaiah 3:5). Job will return to the young men who mock him in 30:1–12.

a: I got away with only the skin of my teeth.
p: The English idiom 'by the skin of my teeth' comes from this verse, but what Job meant is unclear.
b: The English phrase, meaning "just barely", entered the language through the Geneva Bible (1560) and the KJV. In Hebrew be'or shinnay probably means "with nothing": teeth have no skin, so Job has escaped with nothing at all; or it means his gums, all that is left of him; or, as some read it, his lips, his one means of speech. Some see a bitter echo of the Accuser's "skin for skin" (2:4). The first line pictures his wasted body: bones held only by skin. Whatever the exact sense, Job has kept his life and nothing else, as the Accuser was told to spare his life (2:6).
orig: בְּעוֹר שִׁנָּי (be'or shinnay), 'with the skin of my teeth'

a: God's hand has touched me.
p: 'Touch' is the verb of the prologue, when the Accuser asked God to 'touch' Job (1:11; 2:5).
b: The Accuser asked God to reach out his hand and touch everything Job had (1:11), and then to touch his bone and his flesh (2:5). Job does not know about that conversation, but he names the hand rightly: God allowed it (1:12; 2:6). Naga', "touch, strike", also gives nega', "plague". Job's plea for pity (chonnuni, "show me favor") is the cry of the psalms (Psalm 6:2; Psalm 51:1), here turned to friends who should have shown it.

a: never full of eating my flesh
p: In Aramaic 'to eat someone's pieces' meant to slander them. The friends feed on Job with accusations.
b: Job charges the friends with chasing him "like God", as if they had taken God's side in the attack (13:7–8). "Not full of my flesh" may mean they keep devouring him with words: in Aramaic, "to eat the pieces of" someone meant to denounce them, as Daniel's accusers do (Daniel 3:8; Daniel 6:24, where the Aramaic says they "ate the pieces" of the Jews and of Daniel). Psalm 27:2 speaks of evildoers who come "to eat my flesh". The friends feed on Job's misery to support their doctrine.

a: If only someone would put my words in writing
p: Job wants his testimony written down, engraved and filled with lead, so it outlives him and can be read at his trial.
b: Job asks for three kinds of permanence: a written record (sefer, a document or inscription), an inscription engraved with an iron tool, and letters cut into rock and filled with lead, or perhaps written on a sheet of lead. Kings carved their deeds in cliffs to last forever, as Darius I did at Behistun in Persia (about 520 BC), and lead was used for writing in the ancient world. Job's words are meant as legal testimony, so that after his death the case can still be heard. The irony is that his wish was granted: his words have been written down and read for more than two thousand years, in this book.

a: As for me, I know that my redeemer lives
p: Christ and the resurrection; God clearing Job in life; a heavenly advocate; or Job's own cry. See the chapter page.
b: These are the most debated verses in Job, and the readings answer two questions at once: who the go'el is, and when Job is cleared. 1. Resurrection and Christ. The redeemer is God, whom Christians know in Christ, and Job sees him in his own risen body; this is the reading of the Greek and Latin translations, most church fathers, Handel's Messiah, and modern scholars such as Andersen. 2. Vindication within life. The redeemer is God, who will clear Job while he is still "in my flesh", as he does in 42:7–17 (Gordis, Dhorme; the Jewish Publication Society version). 3. The witness of 16:19. A heavenly advocate will take Job's side, perhaps after his death (Mowinckel, Pope, Habel). 4. Job's own cry. Job's testimony, personified, will plead for him (Clines).

a: my redeemer
p: Go'el is the kinsman who rescues family: buys back land and people, avenges blood. The Plain keeps 'redeemer', lowercase.
b: A go'el is the nearest male relative whose duty is to rescue his kin: to buy back family land (Leviticus 25:25), to buy back a relative sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49), and to avenge a murder as "the avenger of blood" (Numbers 35:19). Elsewhere this site has "family redeemer" for Boaz (Ruth 3:9). Here the Plain has "my redeemer" for three reasons. It keeps the link with that family word, and with God as Israel's Redeemer (Isaiah 41:14; Psalm 19:14). "Vindicator" or "defender" would pick out only the legal task, though avenging blood (16:18) and clearing Job's name are surely part of it. And "family redeemer" would decide that the go'el is a relative, when Job's relatives have just abandoned him (19:13–19). It is lowercase because who is meant is the question.
orig: גֹּאֲלִי חָי (go'ali chai), 'my redeemer is alive'
r: Leviticus 25:25; Leviticus 25:47–49; Numbers 35:19; Ruth 3:9; Ruth 4:4–6; Isaiah 41:14; Psalm 19:14; Proverbs 23:10–11; 16:18; 19:13–19

a: I know that my redeemer lives
t: Handel, the funeral service and the hymns
p: Through the Latin funeral office, the Prayer Book burial service and Handel's Messiah, this line became a Christian hymn of resurrection.
b: The Latin Office of the Dead read Job 19:20–27 at night prayer for the dead, and a responsory sang, "I believe that my redeemer lives, and on the last day I will rise from the earth." The Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1662) opens its burial service with 19:25–27 in procession, and the Catholic funeral lectionary offers 19:1, 23–27 as a reading. In 1741 Charles Jennens set the KJV words at the start of Part III of Handel's Messiah, joined to Paul's "now is Christ risen from the dead, the firstfruits of them that sleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20, KJV). The soprano air "I know that my Redeemer liveth" is the music shown in the hands of Handel's statue on his monument in Westminster Abbey. Samuel Medley's hymn (1775) begins with the same words.

a: and at last he will stand up on the dust
p: Acharon may mean 'at last, in the end', 'afterward', or a title: 'the Last' one, the one who has the final word.
b: Ve'acharon is an adjective, "last, later". Used as an adverb it means "at last, in the end" (compare the related ba'acharonah, "afterward", in Deuteronomy 13:9), which most translators follow and the Plain keeps. But it can also describe the redeemer: "as the Last", the one who outlasts everyone. God calls himself "the first and the last" (acharon) in Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12. In a court, "the last" may be the one who speaks last and so decides the case, or the one who comes after Job dies, his survivor and avenger. The KJV's "at the latter day" (with "day" in italics, as a supplied word) and the Vulgate's "on the last (day)" read it as the end of time, which the Hebrew does not say but does not rule out.

a: he will stand up on the dust
p: 'Dust' may be the earth, Job's grave, or the ash heap where he sits. 'Stand up' is the word for a witness rising in court.
b: 'Al-'afar can be "on the earth" (41:33 has the same phrase), as most versions take it. But in Job 'afar is also the dust of the grave (7:21; 17:16; 20:11; 21:26) and the dust of mourning in which Job sits (2:8, 12; 16:15; 42:6). So the redeemer may stand on the earth, or over Job's grave, or beside Job in his dust. Yaqum, "he will rise, stand up", is used of a witness taking the stand (Deuteronomy 19:15–16; Psalm 27:12; Psalm 35:11), which fits the trial language of 16:19 and 19:23–24. The Greek and the Vulgate make the verb refer to raising Job (see the variants).
orig: עַל־עָפָר יָקוּם ('al-'afar yaqum), 'on dust he will rise'

a: Even after my skin has been stripped off like this
p: The Hebrew says 'after my skin they have struck off, this'. The KJV's 'worms destroy this body' is not in the Hebrew.
b: Literally: "and after my skin they have struck off this". Niqqefu is used of cutting down trees (Isaiah 10:34), so "struck off, stripped off". "This" may point at his ruined body, "this (skin of mine)", or mean "thus". "After my skin" may be time ("after my skin has been destroyed") or place ("behind my skin", that is, inside it). The KJV printed "And though after my skin worms destroy this body" with "though", "worms" and "body" in italic type, its sign for words the translators supplied. That wording, sung in Handel's Messiah, made the verse sound like the decay of a corpse in the grave, which the Hebrew does not say so plainly.

a: from my flesh I will see God
p: The Hebrew 'from my flesh' can mean 'from within my flesh', in the body, or 'away from my flesh', without it.
b: Mibbesari is the crux. The preposition min can mean "from the vantage of": "from my flesh", looking out from within his body. That is how the Vulgate ("in my flesh"), the KJV and the resurrection reading take it, and also the reading of vindication in this life ("while still in my flesh", as the Jewish Publication Society version renders it). But min can also mean "apart from", as in 11:15 and 21:9: "without my flesh I will see God", after death, as a spirit. Both senses are possible grammar. The Plain keeps "from", which leaves the question open as the Hebrew does. The verb chazah, "see, behold", is used of visions (Isaiah 1:1).

a: I will see God
p: Job's deepest hope is not restored health but to see God. It comes true in 42:5, in a way he did not expect.
b: What Job longs for is to see God face to face and to be seen as innocent. The Psalms share the hope: "But I, in the right, will look upon your face. When I wake up, I will be filled with the sight of your form" (Psalm 17:15). In the end it happens: Job, who had only heard of God, says that now his eye sees him (42:5). Christians link the verse with the hope of seeing God after death or at the resurrection: "Blessed are those whose hearts are pure, because they will see God" (Matthew 5:8), and "we will see him just as he is" (1 John 3:2).
r: 42:5; Psalm 17:15; Psalm 11:7; Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2; 1 Corinthians 13:12; Revelation 22:4

a: my own eyes will see, and not a stranger
p: Either 'I, and not someone else, will see', or 'God will not be a stranger to me'.
b: Velo zar, "and not a stranger", can be read three ways. Not another person: Job himself will see, not someone else on his behalf (KJV "and not another"; Vulgate et non alius), stressing that it will be Job in person. Not as an enemy: zar can mean a hostile outsider, so God will no longer be a stranger to him, as he has been through all these chapters (19:11, "he treats me as one of his foes"). Not a stranger's eyes: "my eyes, not a stranger's". The first and second can both be true: the man whose house treats him as a stranger (19:15) will meet a God who does not.

a: My inmost being is spent with longing!
p: Literally 'my kidneys are spent in my chest': Job is worn out with longing for that day.
b: The Hebrew says "my kidneys (kilyotay) are finished in my bosom". The kidneys were the seat of the deepest emotions (16:13; Psalm 73:21). Kalah, "to be spent, finished", is used of longing so strong it wears one out: "My being yearns, and even wastes away, for the LORD's courtyards" (Psalm 84:2); "My soul is spent with longing for your salvation" (Psalm 119:81). Job's certainty in 19:25 does not take away his pain; it makes him ache for what he is sure is coming.
orig: כָּלוּ כִלְיֹתַי בְּחֵקִי (kalu khilyotay becheqi), 'my kidneys are spent in my bosom'

a: so that you may know there is judgment
p: The last word, shaddun, is unclear: 'that there is a judgment', or possibly 'the Almighty' (Shaddai).
b: Job turns the warning around: the friends who hunt him should fear the sword themselves, for their fury is a crime that earns it. The last word is read (Qere) shaddun and written (Ketiv) shaddin. Most read it as she-din, "that there is judgment", using a short form of "that" and the Aramaic-style word din, "judgment". Others read Shaddai, "so that you may know the Almighty", or "the Judge". The Greek has something else entirely. Either way, Job's hope of a court in heaven (16:19; 19:25) is also a warning to those who judge him unfairly: they too will be judged, as God's rebuke in 42:7–8 confirms.

a: So my restless thoughts push me to reply
p: Zophar admits he speaks from agitation. He has heard Job's warning (19:29) as an insult.
b: Se'ippay, "my disquieting thoughts", is the word Eliphaz used for the troubled thoughts before his night vision (4:13). Chushi is "my haste, my agitation". Zophar is honest about his feelings: Job's warning that the friends should fear the sword (19:28–29) has stung him, and he feels he must answer. He does not respond to Job's great hope in 19:25–27 at all; he returns to the fate of the wicked, which he takes to be the real issue.

a: and a spirit from my own insight answers for me
p: Like Eliphaz with his night spirit (4:15), and Elihu later (32:8), Zophar claims that a 'spirit' prompts his answer.
b: "Spirit" (ruach) may simply be Zophar's own mind and temper, or he may claim a kind of inspiration. Eliphaz said a spirit passed before his face in the night (4:15–16), and Elihu will say it is the spirit in a person, the breath of the Almighty, that gives understanding (32:8, 18). Each speaker claims authority beyond his own opinion. The Old Greek lacked this verse; it was filled in from Theodotion.

a: The cheering of the wicked is close to its end
p: The wicked may prosper, but only briefly. Many psalms say the same thing, and it is the point Job will attack in chapter 21.
b: Zophar's claim is not that the wicked never prosper, but that their success is short and ends in ruin. This is mainstream biblical wisdom: "Do not burn up inside over people who do evil... For they will soon dry up like grass" (Psalm 37:1–2); the psalmist envied the wicked "until I came into the holy places of God and gave thought to where they end up" (Psalm 73:17–20). Zophar appeals to what has always been known "from ancient times" (20:4; compare 8:8–10; 15:18). His speech is vivid and morally serious. Its weakness is that it admits no exceptions, and Job answers with the exceptions (21:7–34).

a: Even if his greatness climbs to the sky
p: The proud man who reaches for heaven and is brought down is a classic biblical picture: Babel, the king of Babylon.
b: The builders of Babel wanted a tower with its top in the heavens (Genesis 11:4). The king of Babylon said, "I will climb above the heights of the clouds", and was brought down to Sheol (Isaiah 14:13–15). Obadiah warns Edom, Job's own region, that though it soars like an eagle God will bring it down (Obadiah 3–4). The Greek reads differently: "if his gifts go up to heaven, and his sacrifice touches the clouds", turning pride into religious display.

a: he will vanish for good, like his own manure
p: A crude, deliberate insult: the proud man ends like his own excrement, swept away and forgotten.
b: Gelel is dung. The Bible uses the image for total, shameful removal: God will sweep away the house of Jeroboam "the way someone sweeps out dung, until it is finished" (1 Kings 14:10), and the bodies of the wicked will lie "like dung" (Zephaniah 1:17). The contrast with 20:6 is sharp: the head in the clouds ends in the dung heap. Some have tried to soften the word to "like his own figure" or "in his glory", but the crude sense fits Zophar's style.

a: Like a dream he takes flight, and no one can find him
p: The wicked vanish like a dream on waking. Psalm 73 uses the same image of the wicked.
b: "Like a dream to someone who has woken, Lord, when you get up, you will scorn their image" (Psalm 73:20). Isaiah pictures Jerusalem's enemies vanishing "like a dream, like a vision in the night" (Isaiah 29:7). Zophar picks up words Job used of his own life: the eye that sees him will see him no more (7:8), and his place will not know him again (7:10). Job said that of every mortal; Zophar says it is the fate of the wicked.

a: His sons will have to make it up to the poor
p: Either his sons must appease the poor he wronged, or, with other vowels, the poor will crush his sons.
b: Yeratsu dallim is usually read from ratsah, "to be pleased, to pay off": his sons must seek the favor of the poor, or pay them back. With other vowels, from ratsats, "to crush", it says "the poor will oppress his sons", which is the Greek's sense too ("may his inferiors destroy his sons"). Either way, the children pay for the father's wrongs. Job will answer this doctrine sharply in 21:19–21.

a: His bones were brimming with young strength
p: The word 'alumim means 'youth'. The KJV took it as 'the sin of his youth', and some read 'his hidden sins'.
b: 'Alumav (Ketiv singular, Qere plural) is from 'elem, "young man", so "his youthful vigor": he dies in his prime, and his strength lies down in the dust with him. The Vulgate has "the vices of his youth" (vitiis adolescentiae), and the KJV followed it, adding "the sin of" in italics: "full of the sin of his youth". Others connect the word with 'alam, "to hide", as in "our hidden sins" (Psalm 90:8), giving "his bones are full of his hidden sins". The Greek has "youth", though the Old Greek lacked the verse and Origen filled it in from Theodotion. The Plain follows the plain sense of the Hebrew.

a: Evil may be sweet to his taste
t: Sweet food that turns to poison
p: Zophar's long food picture: the wicked savor evil like a sweet, but it turns into snake venom in the stomach.
b: In 20:12–23 Zophar builds one extended image. The wicked man rolls evil around his mouth like a treat, holds it under his tongue, will not let it go. In his stomach it turns to "the gall of cobras". He vomits up the wealth he swallowed (20:15), and in the end God "rains" anger on him as his meal (20:23). Proverbs uses the same idea: "To a man, bread from lying is sweet, / but afterward his mouth gets filled with grit" (Proverbs 20:17), and "Water you steal tastes sweet" (Proverbs 9:17). Revelation's scroll sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach is a different image (Revelation 10:9–10).

a: an adder's tongue slays him
p: Many ancients thought snakes killed with their tongues, so the tongue stands for the venom.
b: Ancient writers often believed a snake's sting was in its forked tongue. The Bible uses the same picture: "They whet their tongues like a snake; under their lips lies the venom of the viper" (Psalm 140:3), and Psalm 58:4 compares the wicked to a deaf cobra. Zophar's point is that the wicked man's evil comes back to him as poison. The words for snakes, peten (cobra) and ef'eh (viper or adder), cannot be matched exactly with modern species.

a: the rivers in flood with honey and butter
p: Honey and curds were the food of a rich land. The wicked man will never enjoy them.
b: "Honey" is wild honey or date syrup, and chem'ah is curds or butter, the soured milk product of herding peoples. Together they stood for abundance: the land "flowing with milk and honey" (Exodus 3:8), the honey and curds of Deuteronomy 32:13–14, and the "curds and honey" of Isaiah 7:15, 22. Job says that in his good days his steps were washed in butter (29:6). The wicked man in Zophar's poem will not live to see such plenty.

a: He broke the poor and left them to themselves.
p: Zophar's wicked man crushed the poor and seized houses. Eliphaz will soon accuse Job of exactly this (22:6–9).
b: The crimes of 20:19–21 are those the prophets condemn: crushing the poor, seizing houses (Micah 2:2; Isaiah 5:8), insatiable greed. Zophar does not name Job, but for the friends Job's ruin must have a cause, and in his next speech Eliphaz will say it outright, accusing Job of sending widows away empty (22:9). Job's reply comes in his oath of innocence: he rescued the poor, was eyes to the blind and a father to the needy (29:12–17; 31:16–22).

a: and rain it on him for his meal
p: The man about to fill his stomach is fed God's anger instead, as at the quails in the wilderness.
b: The word bilchumo is uncertain: "as his food" (from lechem), "into his flesh", or "on his body". The scene recalls the quails in the wilderness: while the meat was still in their mouths, God's anger rose and struck them (Numbers 11:33; Psalm 78:30–31). God "raining" judgment is also the language of Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and of Psalm 11:6, "On the wicked he will rain down traps, / fire and sulfur." Zophar says God will feed the glutton with wrath.

a: a bow of bronze shoots him through
p: He escapes one weapon only to be hit by another. A 'bronze bow' is a bow strengthened with bronze, or an arrow tipped with it.
b: The Iron Age brought iron swords and spearheads, but bronze was still used for arrowheads and for fittings on bows. "A bow of bronze" appears in David's song (2 Samuel 22:35; Psalm 18:34), probably a composite bow with bronze bindings, a very powerful weapon. The picture is of no escape: "as when a man runs from a lion, and a bear comes at him" (Amos 5:19). The arrow passes right through and out of his back, and its flashing tip comes out of his gallbladder (20:25). Job used the same organ for God's archers (16:13).

a: A fire no one blew on will swallow him
t: Fire not lit by human hands
p: Fire that no one fanned is fire from God. Job's readers remember 'the fire of God' that burned his flocks (1:16).
b: A fire that needs no bellows or breath to start it is divine fire, like the fire that came out from the LORD on Nadab and Abihu and on Korah's men (Leviticus 10:2; Numbers 16:35). Zophar's poem keeps drawing near to Job's story: in 1:16 "the fire of God fell from the sky" and burned up Job's sheep and servants, and his tent, his children's house, was destroyed (1:19). "It will go badly for anyone left in his tent" fits Job's case cruelly well. The Old Greek has "may a stranger afflict his house" in the next verse.

a: The sky will lay his sin bare
p: Job appealed to earth and to a witness in heaven (16:18–19). Zophar says both will testify against the wicked.
b: This verse is Zophar's reply to Job's two great appeals. Job cried, "Earth, do not hide my blood" and "my witness is in heaven" (16:18–19). Zophar turns both around: heaven will expose the guilt of the wicked, and the earth will "take its stand" (mitqomemah, the root of yaqum in 19:25) against him. In Israel's covenant tradition heaven and earth are called as witnesses (Deuteronomy 30:19; Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2). Zophar is sure which way their testimony will go; the book's ending suggests he was wrong about Job.

a: swept off like streams on the day of his anger
p: The verbs may picture goods carried off into exile, or a flood that washes a house away.
b: Yigel may be from galah, "to go into exile, be carried off": what his house has produced will be taken away as plunder. Niggarot means things that pour out, torrents (2 Samuel 14:14 uses it of spilled water). Some read the line as a flood: "a torrent will carry off his house". "His anger" is God's, at the "day" of judgment (compare 21:30). The Greek has "may destruction drag his house to the end".
orig: יִגֶל יְבוּל בֵּיתוֹ נִגָּרוֹת (yigel yevul beto niggarot)

a: This is the share God gives a wicked person
p: A closing summary like Bildad's (18:21). Its first line comes back in nearly the same Hebrew in 27:13.
b: Zophar ends with a formula: "This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the inheritance of his word from God." "Share" (cheleq) and "inheritance" (nachalah) are land-holding words: as Israel received its share of the land, the wicked receive their share of doom. Bildad ended the same way (18:21), and so does Eliphaz in his own fashion (15:34–35). Strikingly, nearly the same line opens 27:13–23, in a speech under Job's name, which is one reason scholars think the third cycle is disordered. The Greek calls God "the Overseer" (episkopos) here.

a: and let this be all the comfort you offer
p: The friends came to comfort (2:11). Job asks for one comfort only: that they listen.
b: Eliphaz had offered "the comfort God gives" (15:11). Job turns the word around: the best consolation (tanchumot) they can give is to hear him out. Silence was their first and best act of friendship, when they sat with him seven days and said nothing (2:13). The chapter ends with the same word: "How then can you comfort me with puffs of air?" (21:34).

a: once I am done, go on and sneer
p: 'Sneer' is singular in Hebrew, aimed at one friend, probably Zophar, who has just spoken.
b: The verbs in 21:2–3 are mostly plural, but talʿig, "you may mock", is singular. Job seems to turn to Zophar, whose speech has just ended, or to whichever friend speaks next. The Greek and some other versions make it plural. Job does not expect to persuade them; he asks only to be heard first.

a: As for me, is my complaint aimed at a man?
p: Job's quarrel is not with the friends but with God, which is why he cannot be patient.
b: Siach, "complaint", is the word of 7:13 and 10:1. Job says his complaint is not against a human being, who could be answered or ignored. It is against God, and God has not answered. That is why his "temper runs short" (literally "my spirit is short", the opposite of patience; compare Exodus 6:9; Micah 2:7). Christians who call Job a model of patience (James 5:11) have to reckon with this verse; James's word is better translated "endurance".

a: and put a hand over your mouth
p: A gesture of shocked or awed silence. Job will make the same gesture before God (40:4).
b: To lay one's hand on one's mouth is to fall silent in the face of something overwhelming: the princes did so when Job came into the gate (29:9), the nations will do so at God's deeds (Micah 7:16), and Proverbs advises it to anyone who has played the fool (Proverbs 30:32). Job tells the friends to look at him and be struck dumb. At the end, faced with God's speeches, Job will lay his own hand on his mouth (40:4).

a: Why do the wicked stay alive
p: Job's question is asked across the Bible and in older Babylonian poems. Job asks it as a test of the friends' claim.
b: Jeremiah asks, "Why does the way of the wicked go well?" (Jeremiah 12:1). The psalmist nearly lost his footing as he "watched the wicked thrive" (Psalm 73:3–12), and Habakkuk asks why God is silent while the wicked swallow the righteous (Habakkuk 1:13). Ecclesiastes notes a wicked man living long in his wickedness (Ecclesiastes 7:15). The question is older than Israel: the Babylonian Theodicy, a dialogue poem perhaps from about 1000 BC, has the sufferer complain that those who neglect the god prosper while the devout grow poor. Job's question directly answers Zophar's claim that the triumph of the wicked is short (20:5).
r: 20:5; Jeremiah 12:1; Psalm 73:3–12; Habakkuk 1:13; Malachi 3:15; Ecclesiastes 7:15; Ecclesiastes 8:14

a: Their children stand firm in front of them
p: Bildad said the wicked leave no descendants (18:19). Job says he has seen the opposite.
b: Job answers the friends point by point. Bildad: no child or grandchild (18:19). Job: their children are settled around them (21:8). Bildad: terrors on every side (18:11). Job: their homes are at peace (21:9). Eliphaz: their vine drops its grapes (15:33). Job: their bull breeds and their cows calve (21:10). Zophar: his sons will pay back the poor (20:10). Job: their children dance (21:11). The contrast with Job's own dead children (1:18–19) is left unsaid, which makes it louder.

a: no rod from God comes down on them
p: The rod is God's punishment. Job had begged God to take his rod off him (9:34); the wicked never feel it.
b: The shevet is a rod or staff, used for discipline (Proverbs 13:24) and as a picture of God's punishment: "I will call their rebellion to account with the rod" (Psalm 89:32).
