Job had asked God to remove his rod from him (9:34). The wicked, by contrast, are not "struck down with everyone else" (Psalm 73:5). Their homes have shalom, peace and safety, "from fear", the very dread that Eliphaz said haunts them (15:21).

a: They raise their voices to drum and lyre
p: The tof was a hand drum, the kinnor a lyre, and the 'ugav a pipe or flute: the music of family celebration.
b: The tof was a frame drum or tambourine, often played by women (Exodus 15:20; 1 Samuel 18:6); the kinnor a hand-held lyre, David's instrument (1 Samuel 16:23); the 'ugav probably a pipe or flute, first named in Genesis 4:21. Job uses the same three for his own turned-to-mourning music (30:31). The scene is a happy household, children dancing, nothing like the empty tent of Bildad's wicked man (18:15).

a: and they go down to Sheol in an instant
t: In an instant, or in peace?
p: Rega' is 'a moment' (a quick, painless death) or, from another root, 'peace'. The Greek has 'in the rest of Hades'.
b: Uvrega' usually means "in a moment": the wicked die quickly, without long suffering. A second root raga', "to be at rest", gives "in peace", and the Greek has "they fell asleep in the rest of Hades". Either way, their death is easy, the opposite of Job's slow agony. In the first line the written text (Ketiv) has yevallu, "they wear out (their days)", and the reading tradition (Qere) yekhallu, "they complete"; the sense is the same. Psalm 73:4 says the wicked have "no pangs" in death.

a: They tell God, "Go away from us.
p: The wicked say to God: leave us alone; why serve you? Pharaoh said the same, and so do the scoffers in Malachi.
b: The speech of 21:14–15 is practical atheism: not denying God exists, but saying that he does not matter. Pharaoh asked, "Who is this LORD, that I should heed his voice?" (Exodus 5:2). Proverbs fears that wealth will lead a person to say, "Who is the LORD?" (Proverbs 30:9), and the people of Malachi say, "Serving God is worthless" (Malachi 3:14). The line "What do we get?" answers the Accuser's question in 1:9, whether Job fears God "for nothing". For the book's first readers, small and poor beside rich neighbors, the question was real. Eliphaz will quote this speech back at Job in 22:17.

a: Yet see, their good fortune is not theirs to hold.
p: Either Job grants that the wicked do not control their own prosperity, or it is a question: 'Is not their wealth in their own hands?'
b: Read as a statement (as the Plain), Job grants a point: the prosperity of the wicked is not their own doing but God's gift, which makes it more troubling. Then he separates himself from them: "The plans of the wicked are far from me!". Read as a question, "Is not their good fortune in their own hands?", it continues Job's protest. Some take the second line as Job quoting a pious formula the friends would use. The same line comes again in 22:18, where Eliphaz throws it back at Job. Whatever the reading, Job never adopts the creed of 21:14–15 himself.

a: How many times does the wicked man's lamp go dark?
p: Job quotes Bildad's proverb (18:5) and asks how often it actually happens.
b: "The lamp of the wicked will be put out" was a proverb (Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 24:20), and Bildad used it (18:5–6). Job asks a factual question: how often? This is a new move in the debate. Job appeals to experience against tradition, to what anyone can observe, rather than to what the fathers taught (8:8–10; 15:18). "Pains" (chavalim) are birth pains, or with another sense of the word, "portions", what God "apportions". The answer Job expects is: hardly ever.

a: like husks that a whirlwind steals
p: Psalm 1 says the wicked are like chaff the wind blows away. Job asks whether that ever happens.
b: At threshing, grain was tossed in the air so the wind would carry off the light husks, the chaff. "The wicked are not like this. No, they are like the husks the wind drives off" (Psalm 1:4); compare Psalm 35:5, Isaiah 17:13 and Hosea 13:3. Job asks, "Are they ever?" The question challenges the friends' version of the doctrine, which Psalm 1 also teaches. The rest of the Bible keeps both: the wicked do perish (Psalm 1), and they often prosper long (Psalm 73), and the answer is God's final judgment.

a: "God stores up a man's guilt for his children"?
p: Job quotes the friends' answer, that the children will pay, and rejects it: let the guilty man pay himself.
b: The Hebrew has no "you say"; the Plain uses quotation marks to show that Job is citing a saying, as most translators agree. It was a real teaching: the LORD says, "I bring the fathers' guilt home to the children" (Exodus 20:5; compare Exodus 34:7), and Zophar applied it (20:10). Job finds it unjust: what does the dead man care about his family after him (21:21)? Deuteronomy already limits it in human courts (Deuteronomy 24:16), and in the exile Jeremiah and Ezekiel reject the proverb "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb" (Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:2–4, 20). Readers after the exile, who felt they were paying for their parents' sins, would have heard their own debate here.
r: Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:7; 20:10; 21:21; Deuteronomy 24:16; Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:2–4; Ezekiel 18:20; Lamentations 5:7; John 9:2–3

a: let him drink down the Almighty's fury
p: To drink God's anger is a prophetic picture of judgment, as if from a cup.
b: Judgment as a cup that the guilty must drink is a common biblical image: "For the LORD holds a cup in his hand... its dregs they will drain and drink, all the wicked of the earth" (Psalm 75:8); Jerusalem drank "the cup of his fury" (Isaiah 51:17); and the nations are given "this cup, the wine of rage" (Jeremiah 25:15). Revelation uses it of the final judgment (Revelation 14:10). Jesus speaks of the cup he must drink (Mark 14:36). Job wants the wicked to drink it themselves, and see it with their own eyes, rather than pass it on to their children.

a: Will someone instruct God about knowledge
p: This may be Job quoting the friends' objection, or Job's own point that God is beyond being taught.
b: Some read 21:22 as the friends' objection, which Job quotes: "Who are you to teach God? He judges even the angels." Then 21:23–26 is his reply: God may judge the heavens, but on earth he treats the good and the wicked alike. Others hear Job's own voice: he is not trying to teach God, only to report what he sees. "The lofty ones" (ramim) are heavenly beings (compare 4:18; 15:15; 25:2). Isaiah asks, "Who taught him knowledge?" (Isaiah 40:14), and Paul, "Who has come to know the Lord's mind?" (Romans 11:34).

a: His pails overflow with milk
p: The word 'atin occurs only here. It may be 'pails' or a part of the body; the Greek has 'his insides are full of fat'.
b: 'Atinav is a hapax, a word found once. Later Hebrew and Aramaic have a similar word for olive vats or pails, which gives "his pails are full of milk", a picture of rich herds. But the parallel line, "the marrow of his bones", suggests a body part, and the Greek and the Vulgate read "his insides (or sides) are full of fat"; some modern versions have "his body is well fed". Either way the man dies sleek and well fed, unlike the man of 21:25.

a: Both lie down in the same dust
p: The happy man and the bitter man end in the same grave. Ecclesiastes makes the same observation.
b: Job's point is that death shows no moral pattern. One man dies at ease, another in bitterness, and the maggot covers both (compare 17:14; Isaiah 14:11). Ecclesiastes says the same: "One fate comes to the righteous and to the wicked, to the good, to the clean and to the unclean" (Ecclesiastes 9:2), and the wise man dies just like the fool (Ecclesiastes 2:14–16). For Job, that is not resignation but protest: if death ends everything, then justice must be done before it, or there is none. That is part of why 19:25–27 reaches beyond it.

a: Whatever became of the nobleman's house
p: The friends point to the ruined house of the tyrant. Job's readers know whose house fell (1:19).
b: Nadiv, "noble, prince", is said with irony: the "nobleman" here is the rich tyrant whose house God destroys. The friends' argument is: look around, the houses of the wicked always fall. But the one house that has collapsed in the book is the house of Job's eldest son, on all Job's children (1:19). Job feels the hidden accusation, as he says in 21:27. His answer is to appeal to people who travel (21:29), who have seen many lands and know better.

a: Haven't you questioned people passing along the road?
p: Travelers had seen the world. Job appeals to their wider experience against the friends' village wisdom.
b: In a world without newspapers, merchants and travelers brought news from distant places. Job appeals to their "evidence" (ototam, "their signs", the proofs they bring): anyone who has traveled knows that the wicked are often spared and buried with honor. Sirach later praises travel as a source of wisdom: one who has wandered abroad grows shrewd, and he says, "I have seen many things in my travels" (Sirach 31:11–12). Ecclesiastes, too, reports seeing the wicked buried with honor (Ecclesiastes 8:10).

a: that the evil man is spared on the day of disaster
p: The KJV reads the opposite: the wicked are 'reserved to the day of destruction'. Job's argument favors 'spared'.
b: Le-yom ed yechasekh ra' literally reads "to (or for) a day of disaster the evil man is held back". The KJV, following the Vulgate (in diem perditionis servatur malus), took it as "reserved for" a day of doom, which would agree with the friends. Most modern translators read the preposition le- as "on, at" and the verb as "spared, held back from harm": when disaster strikes, the wicked man is kept out of it, and "led away" safe. That fits Job's whole argument in 21:7–33 and the next verses, where no one confronts him and he is buried in honor. Theodotion's Greek, which Origen supplied here, is closer to the Plain: "the wicked is lightened (relieved) in the day of destruction".
orig: לְיוֹם אֵיד יֵחָשֶׂךְ רָע (le-yom ed yechasekh ra')

a: He is borne in procession to the graves
p: The wicked man gets a procession, a guarded tomb and a crowd of mourners: the opposite of the dishonored corpse the friends expected.
b: Lack of burial was a curse (Jeremiah 22:18–19; Isaiah 14:19–20). The friends' theology expects the wicked man's name to die in shame (18:17). Instead, Job says, he is carried in state to the burial ground (qevarot, "graves"), and men keep watch over his gadish, a word for a heap of grain that here seems to mean a burial mound or tomb. Watches were kept over tombs to guard them from robbers and to honor the dead. The Old Greek lacked 21:28–33; Origen filled these verses in from Theodotion.

a: The dirt clods of the wadi lie sweet on him.
p: Even the earth lies gently on him. Tombs were often cut into the sides of wadis, dry valleys.
b: A nachal is a wadi, a valley that fills with water only in the rainy season; tombs were often cut in its rocky sides, as in the Kidron Valley outside Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:6). "Sweet" means the clods lie easy on him: he rests well. Romans later wished their dead "may the earth be light on you", but there is no link between the sayings, just the same human wish. The rest of the verse pictures a vast funeral, or, as some read it, every person who has ever lived going the same way before and after him.

a: What is left of your answers is faithlessness.
p: Ma'al means a breach of trust, the word for unfaithfulness to God. Job says their answers betray both him and God.
b: Ma'al is a strong word: the treachery of a wife (Numbers 5:12) or the sacrilege of Achan (Joshua 7:1), elsewhere on this site "act unfaithfully". Job says nothing remains of the friends' answers except betrayal. They have been unfaithful to him as friends, and, he suggests, to the truth about God (compare 13:7–8, where he asks whether they will tell lies for God). God's verdict in 42:7 agrees in part: the friends have not spoken rightly of him, as Job has. The second round ends with the friends' comfort judged empty, hevel, "puffs of air".
